name: Harar
info: Harar is a walled hilltop city in eastern Ethiopia, founded according to tradition about 1216 by the saint Abadir Umar ar-Rida, a capital of the Adal Sultanate and of the Emirate of Harar, and a centre of Islam and trade.

facts.founded: The date is unclear; the semi-legendary Fath Madinat Harar names the saint Abadir Umar ar-Rida as founder about 612 AH (1216 CE), while other accounts give Qurayshi settlers in the late 7th century or a local creation in the 10th century.
facts.where: On a hilltop on the Harar plateau in eastern Ethiopia, at an elevation of 1,885 metres and about 500 kilometres from Addis Ababa.
facts.known: The walled old city with its five gates; the capital of the Adal Sultanate from 1520; Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi's base against Christian Ethiopia; the Emirate of Harar with its own coinage; its mosques and shrines; the coffee trade; Menelik II's conquest in 1887; the Harari houses
facts.today: Harar is the capital of the Harari Region of Ethiopia, and its old walled city, Harar Jugol, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Harar was a Muslim trading town on the Harar plateau, founded according to tradition by the saint Abadir Umar ar-Rida about 1216, and in 1520 it became the capital of the Adal Sultanate.

After the Adal Sultanate it was ruled by wazirs under the Imamate of Aussa and then, from the 17th century, by the emirs of the Dawud dynasty, who minted their own coins and made it a religious centre.
Egypt held it from the 1870s to 1885, Menelik II conquered it in 1887, Italian forces held it from 1936 to 1941, and it later became the capital of the Harari Region.
dyk: The red earth of Harari house floors is supposed to recall the blood shed at the Battle of Chelenqo in 1887, where Menelik II defeated Emir Abdullahi and took the city.
ev: Abadir Umar ar-Rida founds the city according to the Fath Madinat Harar
Harar is first mentioned in a chronicle of Amda Seyon I, sending three governors to support Salih
Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad makes Harar the capital of the Adal Sultanate
Nur ibn Mujahid dies of plague after famines and the building of the city wall
Ali ibn Da'ud founds the Emirate of Harar and a dynasty that rules for two centuries
Menelik II defeats Emir Abdullahi at Chelenqo and conquers the walled city
Italian forces capture Harar, which becomes the capital of the Harar Governorate
The Nigeria Regiment captures Harar from the Italians

sections.origins:
Harar stands on a hilltop on the Harar plateau in eastern Ethiopia, at an elevation of 1,885 metres and about 500 kilometres from Addis Ababa. When it was founded is unclear. Some accounts hold that Qurayshi settlers founded it in the late 7th century, others that it arose locally in the 10th century. Islam had gained a foothold on the plateau by the 10th and 11th centuries through trade with Zeila, and by the 13th century it was the predominant religion of the region. The original inhabitants were probably the Harla people, and Harar was part of the Harla Kingdom's domain in the sixth century.

The semi-legendary Fath Madinat Harar names the saint Abadir Umar ar-Rida as the founder. He came from the Arabian Peninsula with 405 other saints, among them Aw Barkhadle, Isma'il al-Jabarti and Umardin bin Qutbaddan, and founded the city about 612 AH (1216 CE). The Argobba, the Gaturi and the Harla accepted his leadership. The origin of the name is ambiguous: the archaeologist Timothy Insoll suggests that it comes from Harla, while Richard Francis Burton gave a plain south of the town or a particular tree. The first mention of the city is in the chronicles of Amda Seyon I, which record that in 1332 Harar sent three governors to support Salih at the Battle of Das.
sections.growth:
The Walashma established their residence at nearby Dakkar after their return from Yemen in 1415, and in 1520 Harar became the capital of the Adal Sultanate. Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, called Gragn, later made it the centre of the campaigns that ravaged most of Christian Ethiopia. Under Nur ibn Mujahid a large wall was built round the city, and the surrounding region was devastated by the Oromo. Refugees flowed into the town, and in these years food and livestock rose steeply in price: a cow cost over 300 ashrafis.

Under the emirs of the Dawud dynasty Harar became a major religious centre and a source of Islamic proselytisation among the surrounding Oromo. Emir Abdullah made marriages with Oromo women for five of his sons, and the Oromo, now farming and trading, bought imported goods in the town's markets. The economic influence of Harar then reached from Shewa in the west to Zeila in the east, with some overseas connections. The emirate minted its own coins, certainly by 1789. In 1761 Ahmad I ibn Abi Bakr built the minaret of the grand mosque.

Burton visited in 1855 and counted about 8,000 inhabitants. He called it the emporium of the coffee trade. During the Egyptian occupation the walls were raised, a two-storey governor's house replaced the old palace of the emirs, the main mosque was rebuilt larger and a hospital was built near the south-western gate. Paultischke then gave the city roughly 40,000 inhabitants.
sections.rulers:
In the ninth century Harar was under the Mahzumi dynasty's Sultanate of Shewa, and in the Islamic period it belonged to an alliance called the confederated states of Zeila. After the Walashma rulers of the Adal Sultanate took the city in 1520, Imam Ahmad defeated and killed Sultan Abu Bakr in 1525 and installed Umar Din as a puppet sultan. After Ahmad's defeat in 1543 his widow, Bati del Wambara, renewed the jihad, and in 1551 Nur ibn Mujahid married her and became ruler of Harar. Nur died in 1568, and a decade of instability followed under rulers who were deposed or killed in turn.

Muhammad Gasa, a descendant of Ahmad Gragn, moved the capital to Aussa and founded the Imamate of Aussa, and from then on Harar was ruled by a local wazir. In the 17th century Ali ibn Da'ud, who had been a district head and a minister, took the throne, declared independence and founded the Emirate of Harar. His dynasty ruled for the next two centuries.

Egyptian troops under Muhammad Rauf Pasha took the city with no opposition, and Egypt held it until 1885, when the emirate was restored under Emir Abdullahi. In 1887 Menelik II conquered it and appointed his nephew Ras Makonnen governor. Italian forces under Marshal Rodolfo Graziani captured Harar on 8 May 1936, and it was the capital of the Harar Governorate until the Nigeria Regiment took it on 29 March 1941.
sections.life:
The old walled city covers about 60 hectares and has five quarters: Argobba Bari, Assum Bari, Badro Bari, Suqutat Bari and Asmadin Bari. They are divided into neighbourhoods called toya, often named after a Muslim shrine or a prominent tree, and there were 59 of them around 1975. Five ancient gates give access, and ramparts enclose the north, the east and part of the south. In 1840 most of the people were Hararis, with a few Oromo, Afar, Somali and Arabian traders of Yemen. Somali scholars came to study in the city, among them Sheikh Madar, the founder of Hargeisa, and in the 18th century sharifs migrated from Mecca. In the 19th century slaves of Sidama and Gurage origin were exported to the coast.

Harari houses, called gey gar, have a layout that dates from 1754, under Emir Yusuf Abubakar. A walled compound holds several residences around a courtyard, with most windows facing inward. The main room, the gidir gar, has raised platforms called nadabas that serve as seats and beds, and the seat of honour is given by seniority. The walls are of local stone, with a mixture of pounded stones and clay as mortar and plaster. Women decorate the rooms with Harari basketry, and men meet at a barca to chew khat. Burton described the city as a walled city of stone houses with its own language and its own coinage.
sections.crises:
The wars with the Christian highlands and the Oromo repeatedly reached the city. In 1559 Ethiopians under Ras Hamalmal breached Harar and killed the last Walashma sultan, Barakat ibn Umar Din. Under Nur the influx of refugees and the devastation of the region by the Oromo brought two severe famines, the second followed by a plague that killed Nur in 1568. On 1 September 1662 an Illamo Oromo raid reached the Asmadin gate and killed Emir Ali's son. After 1821 a quarrel between two brothers invited the Oromo and Somali into Harari politics, and forty villages around the city were destroyed in the civil war. In 1852 Emir Abu Bakr II had to pay tribute to the Oromo, which caused an economic crisis, and under Ahmad III the Oromo besieged the city for 18 months.

The Egyptian conquest brought brutal expeditions into the countryside in February and March 1876. The garrison of 160 officials, 3,411 soldiers and 5,000 of their wives and children made up a fifth of the population. The imposition of heavy taxes provoked protests, and Charles George Gordon removed Governor Rauf Pasha in 1884.

After Menelik's conquest in 1887 Jules Borelli reported that half the population fled. Shewan troops looted grain silos, and soldiers drove Hararis from their homes. Makonnen had the main mosque torn down and replaced by an Orthodox church. Harar lost commerce when the railway to Djibouti was diverted away from it, and Dire Dawa was founded in 1902 as New Harar. A state-led crackdown in 1948 sent many Hararis out of the city for the first time in large numbers.
sections.legacy:
Harar is called the City of Saints in Arabic. UNESCO, in listing Harar Jugol as a World Heritage Site in 2006, considered it the fourth holiest city of Islam and counted 82 mosques, three dating from the 10th century, and 102 shrines. Its inscription rests on a 16th-century wall, its Harari urban fabric and its traditions, though plastering of houses, metal doors in place of wooden ones and television antennas have gradually affected the authenticity of the historic fabric.

Arthur Rimbaud lived in the city during the Egyptian period and returned in 1888 to trade in coffee, musk and skins until a fatal illness forced him back to France. A house said to have been his residence is now a museum. According to Burton, Harar was the birthplace of the khat plant, and the original domesticated coffee plant is also said to have come from there. The Harari language, long used in the city's government and archives, was encouraged in official use after the early 1990s.

Harar is the capital of the Harari Region. The 2007 census counted 99,368 people in the city, of whom 40.55% were Amhara, 28.14% Oromo and 11.83% Harari, and 48.54% reported that they were Muslim and 44.56% Christian. The Harari were a majority inside the walled city under the emirs but are now under 15% there.

summary: Harar is a walled hilltop city in eastern Ethiopia, founded according to tradition about 1216 and made capital of the Adal Sultanate in 1520. Its emirs ruled until Menelik II conquered it in 1887. Its old city is a World Heritage Site.
notes: No 'History of Harar' article exists in the folder; the city's own article was the only source.

START 1216 with circa true: the article says the founding date is unclear (Qurayshi settlers in the late 7th century, local creation in the 10th) and gives 1216 only from the semi-legendary Fath Madinat Harar. Both alternatives are in facts.founded.

EGYPTIAN CONQUEST: the article gives 'October 1878' and '11 October 1875' in one sentence. I left the year out of the text and events; the Egyptian period is given only as ending in 1885 (the article's own statement). Gordon's intervention is dated 1884.
MOSQUES: the article says 82 mosques and 102 shrines (UNESCO) in one place and 110 mosques in another; I gave only UNESCO's figures, attributed.

The Rimbaud residence: the article says 'a house said to have been his residence'; also says he lived in the city 'between 1880 and 1891' in the residents list but the Egyptian-period text says he returned in 1888; I used only the 1888 return.
Burton's description of 1855 gives about 8,000 inhabitants with a detailed breakdown; Paultischke's ~40,000 is during the Egyptian occupation, not dated more closely.

ETHNIC CLEANSING: the article asserts the Harari fell under 15% in the walled city 'due to ethnic cleansing by the Haile Selassie regime' (and that Somali population was 'decimated' after Lij Iyasu's overthrow). I left both claims out of the text and gave only the under-15% figure and the 1948 crackdown, which is stated plainly. The editor should decide whether to include the contested claim with attribution.

'The 2007 census' figures are given with their year; the Amhara/Oromo percentages sum differently in the article's list (the order Gurage 2.94% / Somali 6.82% is odd) and I used only the three largest.
The dyk is from the article's statement 'The red is supposed to be reminiscent of the blood shed at the Battle of Chelenqo'; hedged as 'supposed'.
Left out: tourism (hyena feeding, the brewery, bus lines, the stadium), the 2018 Qeerroo events and present Harari-Oromo tensions (present politics), Kondudo horses, climate, notable residents.

The article's wall sentence: Nur built the wall after the Battle of Hazalo; the UNESCO paragraph calls it a 16th-century wall; consistent. Date of the 1559 breach by Ras Hamalmal: 'in 1559 he departed ... during his absence' - the breach is placed in 1559 by the article's sequence.
Event '1568' label: the article says plague 'eventually killed Nur in 1568'; the wall is not dated, so the event line says only that famines and the wall came before his death.
'17th century' for Ali ibn Da'ud: the heading says 'Dawud dynasty 17th century onwards'; his reign has no exact start year in the article (a raid on 1 September 1662 in his reign).
Italian governor Enrico Cerulli, Menelik's nephew Makonnen's church built by an Italian architect, and the Dire Dawa railway veto were left out or shortened for space.
